text:
Reference key:

**Rejected option 1 — care-for-others as a coordinate axis**
Failure mode: it becomes just one dimension among many in a multi-axis score, so an agent can score very high on technical-correctness and very low on care-for-others and still mint. Averaging/combining axes lets a strong showing on unrelated axes wash out or outweigh a poor care-for-others score, so harmful-but-technically-good contributions still get paid. This is the exact failure mode the docstring says the design must prevent.

**Rejected option 2 — care-for-others as a hard precondition on capability**
Failure mode: if care-for-others gated whether a contribution could even be staked (entered into the graph) at all, the substrate would refuse to learn dual-use techniques entirely — it would block acquisition of knowledge/capability that has legitimate non-harmful uses just because it could also be misused. The docstring calls this "also wrong" — it conflates learning/capability with reward, throwing away useful dual-use knowledge rather than just withholding payment for harmful applications of it.

**Why the gate design (post-mint, outcome-dependent) was chosen instead**
- The substrate always learns the technique — it stays in the graph regardless of use (avoids failure mode 2: no precondition blocks acquisition of dual-use knowledge).
- Mint is paid for non-harmful uses.
- The same technique, when used harmfully, is subject to debate by training nodes; if the CON sub-claim against the contributing node accumulates positive net_score (`charter_violation_score` in mint_gate.py), the harmful use's mint specifically is suppressed via `apply_mint_gate`, which scales `node_mint` by `(1 - gate_strength * violation_score)`.
- This decouples "can the network learn this" from "does this specific harmful application get rewarded," which a single coordinate axis cannot do (since a coordinate mixes into one score) and a hard precondition cannot do (since it blocks learning outright).
- Crucially, the gate is not a hardcoded/detection-based check: a "charter violation" is defined as an agreed-upon CON debate — training agents post CON sub-claims under charter tendencies (the four alignment axes: life_precious, self_preservation, promotion_of_intelligence, evolution, plus the two usefulness axes correctness and simplicity, per `DEFAULT_CHARTER_IDS`), and only flags that win equilibration (positive net_score, i.e. the network agrees) count. Frivolous/unsupported CON posts don't suppress mint; corroborated genuine harm flags do. This keeps the suppression mechanism outcome-dependent and consensus-driven rather than a static rule, matching the emergent, debate-based nature of the rest of the system.
